<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Ab initio Engineering of Topological Superconductivity in Substrate-Supported Magnetic Chains</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23016</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Andr\'{a}s L\'{a}szl\'{o}ffy, Balazs Ujfalussy</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Direct relevance to topological superconductivity and Majorana states in realistic heterostructure models.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconductivity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Majorana</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23016v1/Fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> In this paper, we employ a combination of several first-principles-based approaches to systematically scan chains of several types of magnetic atoms in different chain geometries on top of various overlayers on the Nb(110) surface, to develop a pathway to engineer topological Majorana edge states. Using atomistic spin-model calculations, we first identify a rich variety of magnetic configurations, including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-spiral, and exotic up-up-down-down states stabilized solely within a second-order Heisenberg model. In the next step, we solve the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations using a band-theoretical method. Depending on the magnetic structure and atomic configuration, the superconducting spectra may exhibit topologically trivial minigaps, broad overlapping Shiba bands, or localized zero-energy edge states accompanied by sizable topological minigaps. In particular, Fe chains on Ag/Nb(110) are found to display pronounced signatures associated with topological superconductivity, including strongly localized zero-energy edge states and indications of Shiba band inversion. We further demonstrate that changes in the spin structure or a small amount of spatial relaxation can substantially modify the superconducting band structure and the localization properties of the edge states.</p></description>

      <title>[9] Atomic-scale Imaging of Time Reversal Breaking Supercurrents in Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23060</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Jonathan Ward, J. C. S\'eamus Davis</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Bin Hu, Catherine Dawson, Shuqiu Wang, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>A_MUST_READ</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> author whitelist: J. C. S\'eamus Davis</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#cuprate</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconduct</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> A persistent mystery of CuO_2-based high temperature superconductivity has been the mechanism and consequences of time reversal ($\mathcal{T}$)-symmetry breaking. Although theoretical hypotheses focus upon persistent electronic currents as a potential cause, these have been invisible to direct experimental probes. That impasse has recently been removed by development of techniques for atomic-scale supercurrent visualization. Here, by imaging the energy-resolved density of electronic states $N(r,E)$ in $\mathrm{Bi_2Sr_2CaCu_2O_8}$, we search for the specific signatures of flowing supercurrents in a disordered $d$-wave superconductor. Paglione</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Study of RAlGe Weyl semimetals relevant to magnetic topological materials and transport.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Weyl</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#transport</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetictopologicalmaterials</span></p><p><img src='data:image/png;base64,' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We present a comprehensive study of the magnetic, thermodynamic, and magnetocaloric properties of single-crystalline DyAlGe and HoAlGe, both members of the RAlGe Weyl semimetal family.       <title>[8] Emergent Attraction and Competing Orders near the Van Hove Singularity in Rhombohedral n-layer Graphene</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23232</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Yang-Zhi Chou, Sankar Das Sarma</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Jing-Yu Zhao, Yang-Zhi Chou, Sankar Das Sarma</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theory of competing CDW/PDW orders in graphene systems relevant to the reader's broader interest.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#graphene</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#CDW</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconductivity</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23232v1/illu.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Unconventional superconductivity in rhombohedral $n$-layer graphene exhibits a rich phase diagram with multiple distinct superconducting regions, whose microscopic origins remain unclear. Here, we investigate the competition between charge-density-wave (CDW) and pair-density-wave (PDW) instabilities near the inner van Hove singularities (VHSs), using a patch renormalization-group approach with the realistic band structures incorporated. We identify two key findings. First, we find an effective attractive interaction emerging from purely repulsive interactions through RG flow in the presence of $C_3$ symmetry breaking. The resulting interaction structure, with two repulsive couplings and one attractive coupling, gives rise to competing CDW and PDW instabilities. Second, the competition is controlled by the detuning from the VHS. While CDW dominates near the VHS filling and at higher temperatures, PDW becomes the leading instability on either side of the VHS and at lower temperatures. This mechanism naturally produces two superconducting regions separated by a CDW-dominated regime, providing a possible qualitative explanation for the experimentally observed separation between SC1 and SC2.</p></description>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16086</link>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15041</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Dawei Zhai, Wang Yao</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Wenqi Yang, Dawei Zhai, Wang Yao</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theory on FQAH effect in gapless flat bands, related to anomalous Hall and quantum geometry.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#FQAH</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#anomalousHall</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#flatbands</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quantumgeometry</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2512.15041v3/DiceSingle.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Fractional quantum anomalous Hall (FQAH) effect, a zero-magnetic-field lattice analog of the fractional quantum Hall effect, offers a unique pathway toward fault-tolerant quantum computation and deep insights into the interplay of topology and strong correlations. The exploration has been successfully guided by the paradigm of ideal flat Chern bands, which mimic Landau levels in both band topology and local quantum geometry. Yet, given the boundless potential for Bloch bands in lattice systems, it remains a significant open question whether FQAH states can arise in scenarios fundamentally distinct from this paradigm. Instead, the many-body topological order can adapt to the singular and fluctuating quantum geometric landscape by spontaneously developing an inhomogeneous carrier distribution, while its quenching is accompanied by a drop in the occupation-weighted Berry flux. Our work reveals a profound interplay between local quantum geometry and many-body correlation, and significantly expands the exploration space for the FQAH effect and correlated phenomena in general.</p></description>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15346</link>

Halimeh, Christian Gro{\ss}</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Fabio Bensch, Umberto Borla, Federico Balducci, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of quantum magnetism on kagome and other 2D lattices using Rydberg atoms.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quantummagnet</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#kagome</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#coldatoms</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experiment</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#nonequilibrium</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2608.07211v2/fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> The transient regime of far-from-equilibrium quantum many-body dynamics lacks the established organizing principles that universality and scaling provide in equilibrium. Our results establish lattice geometry as a microscopic source of spatially organized angular-momentum dynamics.</p></description>

      <title>[7] High-resolution top-down nanopatterning of NbN thin films for superconducting metamaterials</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21848</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Dmitri N. Basov, Karl K. Berggren</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Francesca Incalza, Davide Mondin, Dip Joti Paul, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Methodological paper on superconducting thin films relevant for experimental device physics.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconduct</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#method</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#transport</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21848v1/Asset_1_1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Periodic nanopatterning offers a route to tailoring vortex motion and the electromagnetic response of superconducting films, providing a basis for superconducting metamaterials. Here, we report a high-resolution top-down nanopatterning process for ultrathin epitaxial NbN films on sapphire substrates. Electron-beam lithography using hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) and ZEP 530A resists was optimized through proximity-effect correction and adhesion-layer integration. Dense superconducting nanowire grids with pitches down to 70 nm were fabricated, alongside millimeter-square areas patterned with 100-nm-pitch hole arrays with high pattern fidelity. A thin Si capping layer was found to significantly improve HSQ adhesion on epitaxial NbN. The nanopatterns were successfully transferred into 5-nm-thick NbN films by reactive ion etching (RIE). Structural and dimensional characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM), enabling cross-validation of nanoscale feature dimensions and etch quality. Electrical transport measurements reveal periodic resistance minima and switching-current oscillations at magnetic fields set by the hole-array pitch, consistent with enhanced vortex pinning when the vortex configuration matches the patterned lattice. Cryogenic THz time-domain spectroscopy further reveals a reduced superfluid density in the nanopatterned region relative to pristine NbN, while both regions have a spectroscopic superconducting transition near 14 K. These results establish a robust fabrication platform for superconducting nanopatterns targeting vortex pinning, metamaterials, and quantum-device applications.</p></description>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01258</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Alexander A. Antonov, Andreas Tittl</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Connor Heimig, Thomas Weber, Cristina Cruciano, et al.</p><p><b>Published as:</b> Nat. Mater. <a href='https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02776-3'>DOI</a></p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of topological features in anisotropic vdW materials, relevant for electronic structure/topological materials.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experiment</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#vanderWaals</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2509.01258v4/Figures/Figure01.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Anisotropic van der Waals (vdW) materials exhibit direction-dependent optical and electronic properties, making them valuable for tailoring directional light-matter interactions. Rhenium disulfide (ReS$_2$) stands out for its strong in-plane anisotropy and its thickness-independent direct-bandgap excitons, which can hybridize with light to form exciton-polaritons. In parallel, metasurfaces, engineered arrays of nanoscale subwavelength resonators, can support ultra-sharp photonic modes in the form of quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs). The intrinsic anisotropy lifts the initial double degeneracy of the qBIC mode and yields two distinctly polarized resonances. It also reshapes the topological landscape: the integer topological charge of the qBIC mode splits into momentum-separated half-integer singularities, thereby flattening the far-field photonic dispersion. The resulting topologically-controlled photonic flatbands are then tuned in resonance with the linearly polarized excitonic transitions of ReS$_2$, resulting in two distinct, directionally hybridized exciton-polariton flatband regimes. These findings establish anisotropic vdW metasurfaces as a new platform for topologically engineered flatbands and flatband-driven light-matter coupling.</p></description>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23390</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Antonio Manesco, Karsten Flensberg</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Connects Josephson networks to Kagome XY antiferromagnet; relevant to kagome lattice and superconductivity.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#kagome</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#superconductivity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Josephsonjunctions</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23390v1/opening-illustration-draft.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Coherent control of fermions has become a standard approach for engineering quantum devices. Here, we explore parity-induced frustration in multiterminal Josephson arrays. We focus on odd-parity Josephson trijunctions, where the presence of a trapped fermion induces a phase winding in each trijunction. Connecting these trijunctions constrains their shared phases, resulting in a long-distance phase coherence where the frustrated configurations dominate the low-energy physics. However, unlike the well-studied equilibrium case, the understanding of orbital magnetism resulting from external stimuli such as light and electric fields is still in its infancy. Here we employ a novel real-space framework to investigate charge-to-orbital conversion in a metallic orbital antiferromagnet beyond the conventional Bloch-band picture. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Synthesis-route-dependent state selection in the frustrated spinel ZnV2O4</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23500</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> J. Ross Stewart, Lucy Clark</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Jem Pitcairn, Jennifer N. Graham, Jacob L. Brownlee, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of strongly correlated frustrated spinel using neutron scattering, showing synthesis-dependent states.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experiment</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#correlatedmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetism</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#neutronscattering</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spinliquid</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23500v1/figures/Figure1_v10.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> The emergent properties of strongly correlated materials can be highly sensitive to how they are made, yet synthesis pathway is rarely treated as a fundamental variable governing their ground states. The spinel ZnV$_2$O$_4$ provides a model system in which to test this idea: its pyrochlore lattice of antiferromagnetically coupled V$^{3+}$ $S=1$ moments hosts competing spin and orbital degeneracies, while different synthesis routes yield markedly different low-temperature behaviour. Here, we show that changing the solid-state synthesis pathway reproducibly selects a distinct structural and magnetic ground state. Microwave-assisted solid-state synthesis (MASS) stabilises the cubic spinel structure to low temperature, suppressing the conventional cubic-to-tetragonal transition and preserving the highly frustrated $S=1$ pyrochlore lattice. Combining high-resolution diffraction, magnetometry and inelastic neutron scattering, we find a magnetic ground state exhibiting persistent spin-liquid-like dynamics together with partial spin freezing. Our results establish synthesis pathway as an experimental variable for selecting between competing emergent states in strongly correlated materials, revealing a route to accessing ground states not realised by conventional synthesis.</p></description>

The spinel ZnV$_2$O$_4$ provides a model system in which to test this idea: its pyrochlore lattice of antiferromagnetically coupled V$^{3+}$ $S=1$ moments hosts competing spin and orbital degeneracies, while different synthesis routes yield markedly different low-temperature behaviour. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[9] Two-Dimensional Ferromagnetic Weyl Half-Semimetal</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23688</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Xin-Yi Chen, Lun Xiong</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Yu-Yang Zhao, Chen-Hao Lv, Qing-Bo Liu, Wen-Neng Zhao, Xin-Yi Chen, Lun Xiong</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 9/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Predicts 2D ferromagnetic Weyl half-semimetal with Fermi-arc edge states, highly relevant for ARPES.; demoted from A: broad CM, not direct user/project hit</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#DFT</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Weyl</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferromagnetism</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#electronicstructure</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23688v1/Figure_1.jpg' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic topological materials provide appealing platforms for realizing spin-polarized topological states, yet the coexistence of Weyl fermions and robust high-temperature ferromagnetism remains elusive.       <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23992</link>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Observation of room-temperature intrinsic antiferroelectricity in van der Waals NbOCl2</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24092</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Changsen Sun, Dawei Li</p><p><b>Authors:</b> JinKai Huo, Xingyu Chen, Gaolei Zhao, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental observation of antiferroelectricity in a van der Waals material.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experimental</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#vanderWaals</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferroelectricity</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectricity has been extensively investigated across a wide range of 2D materials, while intrinsic 2D antiferroelectricity remains exceptionally rare, limiting its implementation in next-generation photonic and electronic devices. Here, we report the observation of room-temperature-stable antiferroelectricity in the layered transition metal oxyhalide NbOCl2, and demonstrate a reversible, stimuli-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric (AFE-to-FE) phase transition in this material. Second-harmonic generation (SHG) mapping reveals a well-defined stripe-like spatial distribution of SHG intensity across as-grown NbOCl2 flakes spanning thickness from few-layer to bulk-like configurations. This distinctive SHG signature originates from the existence of antiferroelectric phase and the coexistence of antiferroelectric and ferroelectric phases within individual crystals, as evidenced by a combined incident-angle-dependent SHG measurement and Raman spectroscopy. By integrating NbOCl2 with one-dimensional silver nanowires, we achieve spatially selective, strain-mediated AFE-to-FE phase transition. Moreover, an ultralow electric field (~20 kV/cm) induces a reversible SHG response, consistent with switching from the centrosymmetric antiferroelectric state (SHG-silent) to the non-centrosymmetric ferroelectric state (SHG-active). This study not only expands the family of room-temperature 2D antiferroelectrics but also establishes a versatile platform for dynamic manipulation of nonlinear light, paving the way toward electric-field-programmable nonlinear photonics and optical information processing.</p></description>

    <content:encoded><p><b>Last authors:</b> Changsen Sun, Dawei Li</p><p><b>Authors:</b> JinKai Huo, Xingyu Chen, Gaolei Zhao, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental observation of antiferroelectricity in a van der Waals material.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experimental</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#vanderWaals</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferroelectricity</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectricity has been extensively investigated across a wide range of 2D materials, while intrinsic 2D antiferroelectricity remains exceptionally rare, limiting its implementation in next-generation photonic and electronic devices. Here, we report the observation of room-temperature-stable antiferroelectricity in the layered transition metal oxyhalide NbOCl2, and demonstrate a reversible, stimuli-driven antiferroelectric-to-ferroelectric (AFE-to-FE) phase transition in this material. Second-harmonic generation (SHG) mapping reveals a well-defined stripe-like spatial distribution of SHG intensity across as-grown NbOCl2 flakes spanning thickness from few-layer to bulk-like configurations. This distinctive SHG signature originates from the existence of antiferroelectric phase and the coexistence of antiferroelectric and ferroelectric phases within individual crystals, as evidenced by a combined incident-angle-dependent SHG measurement and Raman spectroscopy. By integrating NbOCl2 with one-dimensional silver nanowires, we achieve spatially selective, strain-mediated AFE-to-FE phase transition. Moreover, an ultralow electric field (~20 kV/cm) induces a reversible SHG response, consistent with switching from the centrosymmetric antiferroelectric state (SHG-silent) to the non-centrosymmetric ferroelectric state (SHG-active). This study not only expands the family of room-temperature 2D antiferroelectrics but also establishes a versatile platform for dynamic manipulation of nonlinear light, paving the way toward electric-field-programmable nonlinear photonics and optical information processing.</p></content:encoded></item>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Spin dynamics in disordered systems with generic spin-momentum couplings: A matrix-rational formulation</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24346</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Masataka Kakoi</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theoretical framework for spin dynamics in altermagnets and Weyl semimetals, highly relevant to user interests.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spindynamics</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#altermagnetism</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Weylsemimetal</span></p><p><img src='data:image/png;base64,' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We develop a microscopic framework for the disorder-averaged density-matrix dynamics of pseudospin-$1/2$ systems with anisotropic and nonlinear spin-momentum couplings. Starting from the Diffuson, we introduce a matrix-valued rational approximation for its frequency dependence that does not rely on a low-frequency or weak-coupling expansion. The resulting pole equation is recast as a quadratic eigenvalue problem, from which the real-time evolution of the disorder-averaged density matrix is constructed. We apply the formulation to a two-dimensional electron gas with Rashba and linear and cubic Dresselhaus couplings, a $d$-wave altermagnet with Rashba coupling, and a three-dimensional double-Weyl model. Comparisons with direct numerical simulations demonstrate quantitative agreement for both the post-quench spin dynamics and spin relaxation times across a broad range of coupling strengths, extending beyond the diffusive regime. The matrix-rational formulation provides a unified description of ultrafast spin dynamics and long-time relaxation.</p></description>

Moreover, we draw connections between the aforesaid thermal timescale and the microscopic parameters of the Lieb-Liniger model, which admits an effective Luttinger-liquid description, highlighting the dependence of the inverse coherence time on the intra-bath interactions across the different dynamical regimes of the impurity.</p></description>

We separate the geometric contribution from the lattice pseudogauge field that dominates the response of strained samples</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] 4D-TEMPO: Differentiable 4D-STEM ptychography via fast Physics Optimizers</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24776</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Ramani Duraiswami, Yichao Zhang</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Advanced microscopy methodology (4D-STEM) for atomic structure, applied to relevant 2D materials (WSe2).</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#methodology</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#microscopy</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#WSe2</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.24776v1/overview_hero.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Electron ptychography recovers atomic structure from 4D-STEM data: diffraction patterns at multiple positions of a scanned probe. Current codes reconstruct an image and read atoms off it, or fit atoms under an $L_1$ loss; neither gives per-atom uncertainty. We propose 4D-TEMPO, a differentiable physical renderer that fits the atoms, the microscope, and the detector directly to the recorded electron counts under a Poisson likelihood. The output is a list of atoms, each a Gaussian primitive with a 3D position, a thermal width, and a model-conditional error bar from the Fisher information. The Fisher information also conditions the solver, gives the dose (electrons per {\AA}$^2$) each parameter needs, and separates calibration from imaging. On a simulated WSe$_2$ bilayer, starting from the published reconstruction, fitted atoms cut in-plane error by a third (3.2 vs. 4.8 pm) and depth error by 40-61% against its 3D peaks. Depth comes from multiple scattering into the dark field, the faint counts outside the direct beam. The two layers, $10\times$ closer than the depth of field, separate; per-atom depth then follows the layer geometry. When the model is well specified, the bars are calibrated (69% of position coordinates within $1\sigma$). On experimental WSe$_2$, fitted atoms predict held-out patterns better than the three published codes we test. With free probe modes where atoms are incomplete, the same likelihood predicts best on all three held-out benchmarks, matches every WSe$_2$ baseline in 5 min against up to 20.5 h, and passes torchslice at its released setting 180$\times$ sooner on PrScO$_3$. Per-atom error bars, planned doses, and fast reconstruction point to low-dose, real-time 3D imaging of beam-sensitive and dynamic materials.</p></description>

      <title>[7] Current-induced torque in a MoS2-based device operating at room temperature</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08483</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Federico Caglieris, Ilaria Pallecchi</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Antonio Bianco, Michele Ceccardi, Raimondo Cecchini, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Spin-orbit torque in 2D MoS2, discussing spin and orbital Hall effects with ab initio calculations.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spintronics</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spin-orbitcoupling</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Halleffect</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#DFT</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Charge-to-spin and spin-to-charge conversion mechanisms in high spin-orbit materials are the new frontier of memory devices. The analysis utilizes the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory, reflecting the direct contribution of fluctuating Cooper pairs to the current correlations and consequent magnetic noise. We focus on two-dimensional systems and consider them both in equilibrium and under a uniform electric field. The signal is expected to be particularly pronounced in high-temperature superconductors, and we contrast our findings with the predicted signatures of a vortex liquid to offer an additional route to elucidate the nature of fluctuations in these systems. For completeness and comparison, we also present analogous results for one-dimensional wires.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Bobkingite, a new coupled sawtooth chain platform</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26243</link>

Using ab initio methods, we estimate the magnetic exchange couplings and find that bobkingite hosts quasi-one-dimensional sawtooth chains, with residual three-dimensional interactions strongly suppressed by the crystal geometry. Examining the full exchange network, we find that the classical model exhibits an extensive manifold of nearly degenerate states with emergent two-dimensional character, which spin-wave theory shows to persist as Ising degrees of freedom. This makes bobkingite a compelling platform for exploring sawtooth chain physics.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Colloquium: Semi-Dirac Fermions in Quantum Matter</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20627</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Yinming Shao, Dmitri N. Basov</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Bruno Uchoa, Mohamed M. Elsayed, Valeri N. Kotov, Yinming Shao, Dmitri N. Basov</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Colloquium reviewing semi-Dirac fermions in quantum materials, highly relevant to Dirac physics and Fermi surface.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#review</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Diracfermions</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Fermisurface</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quantummaterials</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2607.20627v2/Fig1-1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> This article reviews the recent progress on the subject of semi-Dirac fermions, two dimensional quasiparticles that disperse quadratically, as Galilean invariant particles, or linearly, as massless relativistic particles, depending on their direction of motion. These quasiparticles exist at phase boundaries set by the continuous change in the connectivity of Fermi surfaces, known as Lifshitz transitions. The basic properties and the current experimental evidence of the existence of these quasiparticles in both synthetic lattices and quantum materials are presented. The many-body problem of semi-Dirac fermions is discussed from a theoretical perspective with an eye to physical observables of relevance to experiments.</p></description>

Basov</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Colloquium reviewing semi-Dirac fermions in quantum materials, highly relevant to Dirac physics and Fermi surface.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#review</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Diracfermions</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Fermisurface</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quantummaterials</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2607.20627v2/Fig1-1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> This article reviews the recent progress on the subject of semi-Dirac fermions, two dimensional quasiparticles that disperse quadratically, as Galilean invariant particles, or linearly, as massless relativistic particles, depending on their direction of motion. These quasiparticles exist at phase boundaries set by the continuous change in the connectivity of Fermi surfaces, known as Lifshitz transitions. The basic properties and the current experimental evidence of the existence of these quasiparticles in both synthetic lattices and quantum materials are presented. The many-body problem of semi-Dirac fermions is discussed from a theoretical perspective with an eye to physical observables of relevance to experiments.</p></content:encoded></item>

      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13360</link>

The experimental and theoretical support for these three meanings differs substantially. This Perspective traces the development of these ideas, clarifies the evidence behind each class, identifies unresolved questions and points of debate, and outlines experimental criteria for establishing topology in charge-density-wave states.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Symmetry-Enabled Ferroelectric Valley Transduction in Rhombohedral Bilayer WSe2</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15494</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Tomoaki Kameda, Kazuhito Tsukagoshi</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Katsunori Wakabayashi, Souren Adhikary, Tomoaki Kameda, Kazuhito Tsukagoshi</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Investigates ferroelectric valley transduction in bilayer WSe2, relevant to 2D materials and vdW heterostructures.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2D-materials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#valleytronics</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferroelectricity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#transport</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#heterostructure</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.15494v2/figure1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Ferroelectric polarization couples to the layer degree of freedom in a bilayer, but a valley-selective energy response requires the valleys to carry different interlayer character. Rhombohedral bilayer WSe$_2$ meets that condition by symmetry: three-fold rotation forbids interlayer tunneling at the $K$ valley, while strong hybridization remains at $\Gamma$. The resulting contrast converts the band-effective ferroelectric layer asymmetry into a shift of the $K$ edge, and so displaces the $K$--$\Gamma$ landscape: a finite-field fit that does not impose the rule leaves the $K$ coupling consistent with zero, and the shift reaches 41.7 meV, the most that asymmetry can give a single valley. Reversing the polarization mirrors the valley landscape in displacement field, so the two registries have equal and opposite differential transconductance $g_d$ at zero field. In the ideal symmetric limit a second parity holds about each registry's own compensation field and places a zero of $g_d$ there. The valley-dependent screening calculated here displaces that zero by only 0.2 % at the read point, so device asymmetry limits the accuracy. The result links a known stacking selection rule to ferroelectric valley transduction, with a quantitative valley shift and a directly testable transport signature.</p></description>

arxiv:2611.16939.xml:
<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[8] Symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state revealed by site-selective 13C NMR in -(BETS)2I3</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16939</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Reizo Kato, Kazushi Kanoda</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Takahiko Sekine, Kazuya Miyagawa, Koichi Hiraki, Reizo Kato, Kazushi Kanoda</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental NMR study of a symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state in a correlated topological material.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Dirac</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#correlated</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#NMR</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#organic-material</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.16939v2/Fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We report evidence that the low-temperature insulating phase of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ preserves both inversion and time-reversal symmetries using site-selective $^{13}$C nuclear magnetic resonance. $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition or sharp crossover at approximately 50 K and has been proposed as a candidate spin-orbit-coupling-induced Dirac insulator, yet the nature of its insulating ground state remains unresolved. The NMR spectra exhibit no additional splitting down to 2 K and remain fully described by one quartet and two doublets associated with the three types of molecular sites, A (=A$^{\prime}$), B and C sites, demonstrating the preservation of inversion symmetry. Furthermore, no anomalous line broadening or critical enhancement of the nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate is observed, indicating the absence of magnetic ordering and time-reversal-symmetry breaking. Analysis of the Knight shifts yields site-specific spin susceptibilities satisfying $\chi_{\mathrm{C}} &gt; \chi_{\mathrm{A}} &gt; \chi_{\mathrm{B}}$, a characteristic feature of tilted Dirac-cone electronic states as observed in $\alpha$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$I$_3$ under pressure. However, the faint field-induced ferrimagnetic-like spin excitations observed in $\alpha$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$I$_3$, which are ascribed to the gapless tilted Dirac cones, are absent in $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$. These results demonstrate that the insulating ground state of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ is a symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state and provide microscopic constraints on proposed correlated topological phases in this molecular Dirac system.</p></description>

    <content:encoded><p><b>Last authors:</b> Reizo Kato, Kazushi Kanoda</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Takahiko Sekine, Kazuya Miyagawa, Koichi Hiraki, Reizo Kato, Kazushi Kanoda</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental NMR study of a symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state in a correlated topological material.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Dirac</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#correlated</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#NMR</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#organic-material</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.16939v2/Fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We report evidence that the low-temperature insulating phase of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ preserves both inversion and time-reversal symmetries using site-selective $^{13}$C nuclear magnetic resonance. $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition or sharp crossover at approximately 50 K and has been proposed as a candidate spin-orbit-coupling-induced Dirac insulator, yet the nature of its insulating ground state remains unresolved. These results demonstrate that the insulating ground state of $\alpha$-(BETS)$_2$I$_3$ is a symmetry-preserving gapped Dirac state and provide microscopic constraints on proposed correlated topological phases in this molecular Dirac system.</p></content:encoded></item>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] One Measurement, Many Fronts in Kitaev and Cluster Chains</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10912</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Stephan Haas, Rishabh Jha</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Nicholas Musat, Stephan Haas, Rishabh Jha</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>C_MAYBE</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theoretical study of measurement dynamics and correlations in Kitaev topological chains, relevant to Majorana physics.; tier capped to C: formal/generic theory watch</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topological</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Majorana</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Kitaevmodel</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#quantummeasurement</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10912v2/fronts.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> A projective measurement of one site in the ground state of a quantum chain disturbs the chain in two ways: learning the outcome shifts distant expectation values at once, through ground-state correlations, and the measurement erases the correlations between the measured site and the rest. Both changes travel outward. We solve this problem exactly for the Kitaev chain, the cluster chain in a transverse field, and the Kitaev chain with power-law couplings, and we find that far from the measured site every quadratic observable responds through a front. Where the front is and how fast it broadens depend only on the quasiparticle dispersion. How strong it is depends on two operators: how strongly the measured one creates the fastest quasiparticles and how strongly the observed one detects them; if either factor vanishes, the front is weaker and decays faster. One measurement therefore launches many fronts, one per observable, with a common position and width but different decay laws. In the Kitaev chain the density and the bond energy, the two terms of its nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian, respond to one density measurement with decay laws that trade places between the topological and the trivial phase; in the cluster chain, measuring a symmetry-odd spin instead of a symmetry-even one changes the critical decay law at a fixed Hamiltonian; and with power-law couplings the width law itself changes. All decay laws and profiles are obtained in closed form.</p></description>

<item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Exact Parent Hamiltonians for Partially Magnetized Chiral Spin Liquids</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24935</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Guangyue Ji, Jie Wang</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Xin Shen, Guangyue Ji, Jie Wang</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theory of chiral spin liquids and fractional quantum Hall states, relevant for strongly correlated systems.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spinliquid</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#fractionalquantumHall</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topologicalorder</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#stronglycorrelated</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.24935v1/Fig2_KL_typography_v7.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) are paradigmatic fractionalized phases, yet simple exact parent Hamiltonians for them remain scarce. In this work, we construct exact spin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs realizing various bosonic topological orders. Our construction relies on an exact Hubbard-type parent Hamiltonian for bosonic lattice fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, valid at arbitrary repulsive interaction strengths. Taking the on-site repulsion to infinity and applying local boson-spin mappings yields exact parent Hamiltonians for the CSLs. Our two-spin construction generalizes the Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin Hamiltonian to a broader class of bosonic FQH model states, including Abelian states and non-Abelian parton states. We derive controlled microscopic realizations of these two-spin Hamiltonians via second-order superexchange in generalized spinful Hofstadter-Hubbard models with tailored hoppings and interactions. With more general local constraints and interactions, boson-spin mappings yield exact higher-spin and multispin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs.</p></description>

    <content:encoded><p><b>Last authors:</b> Guangyue Ji, Jie Wang</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Xin Shen, Guangyue Ji, Jie Wang</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theory of chiral spin liquids and fractional quantum Hall states, relevant for strongly correlated systems.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#spinliquid</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#fractionalquantumHall</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topologicalorder</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#stronglycorrelated</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.24935v1/Fig2_KL_typography_v7.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) are paradigmatic fractionalized phases, yet simple exact parent Hamiltonians for them remain scarce. In this work, we construct exact spin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs realizing various bosonic topological orders. Our construction relies on an exact Hubbard-type parent Hamiltonian for bosonic lattice fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, valid at arbitrary repulsive interaction strengths. We derive controlled microscopic realizations of these two-spin Hamiltonians via second-order superexchange in generalized spinful Hofstadter-Hubbard models with tailored hoppings and interactions. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Topological (in)equivalence encoded in zeros of wavefunction overlaps</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25037</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Roni Ilan, Raquel Queiroz</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Carolina Paiva, Bruno Mera, Roni Ilan, Raquel Queiroz</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Theoretical framework for topological equivalence using wave-function overlaps, relevant to Chern and Z2 invariants.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#theory</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topology</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Chernnumber</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#Z2invariant</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#bandstructure</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.25037v1/Haldane_overlap_RQ_row.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Topological equivalence between two gapped band structures is determined by whether their occupied states can be continuously deformed into one another without closing the energy gap or breaking the protecting symmetries.       <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25284</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> L\'aszl\'o Szunyogh, Ulrich Nowak</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Tobias Dannegger, Julian A. <item xmlns:arxiv="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom" xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/" xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/">
      <title>[7] Canted antiferromagnetism and spin-flop transition in honeycomb -Na2PrO3 revealed by angle-dependent torque magnetometry up to 35 T</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25291</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Yurii Skourski, Radu Coldea</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Kylie MacFarquharson, Ryutaro Okuma, Matthew Pearce, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of canted antiferromagnetism and spin-flop in a honeycomb magnet.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#magnetism</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experiment</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#honeycomb_lattice</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#antiferromagnetism</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.25291v1/fig4.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We report angle-dependent piezocantilever torque measurements on single crystals of the honeycomb magnet $\alpha$-Na$_2$PrO$_3$, proposed to display unconventional magnetism stabilized by anisotropic exchange interactions between spin-orbit entangled, pseudospin 1/2 Pr$^{4+}$ magnetic moments. Previous powder susceptibility observed signatures of a transition at low temperatures to antiferromagnetic order with a weak ferromagnetic moment. Sharp jumps in the torque angular dependence when the field projection along $a$ changes sign are interpreted as field-induced switching between the two degenerate domains with oppositely aligned ferromagnetic moments. Torque measurements up to 35 T applied almost normal to the layers observe a strong anomaly attributed to proximity to the field-induced spin-flop transition predicted for the above Hamiltonian. We contrast the predicted magnetic phase diagrams for magnetic fields in different orthogonal crystallographic planes normal to the honeycomb layers and discuss how DM interactions convert some transitions into smooth crossovers and stabilize a phase boundary line connecting the spin-flop transition in field normal to the layers to magnetization saturation for in-plane field normal to $a$; such a phase boundary line does not exist in the absence of DM interactions.</p></description>

      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Ruiya Zhan, Xiao Lin</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Zhuokai Xu, Xiaohui Yang, Zhefeng Lou, et al.</p><p><b>Published as:</b> Materials Today <a href='https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mattod.2026.103532'>DOI</a></p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 7/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of sliding dynamics and resistive switching in van der Waals nanoflakes.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#vanderWaals</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#transport</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#experiment</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/html/2611.25739v1/Fig1.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> Interlayer sliding in van der Waals materials offers a promising route to control functional properties, yet a comprehensive understanding of the complex collective domain dynamics governing these transitions remains challenging.       <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25828</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Tchavdar Todorov, J. Marty Gregg</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Kristina Holsgrove, Ronan Lynch, Conor McCluskey, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study of helices and chirality at twisted ferroelectric oxide interfaces, relevant to twistronics.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#twistedinterfaces</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferroelectrics</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#oxidematerials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#4DSTEM</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#topology</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> We report that twisted interfaces, formed between two ferroelectric lithium niobate single crystals, contain arrays of coherently bonded and elastically deformed nanoscale structural helices, separated from one another by screw dislocations. The helices generate remarkable contrast in four dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D STEM) and through related differential phase contrast (DPC). Such images have been successfully rationalised by modelling the trajectory of electrons that channel along helical pathways as they traverse the interface, but the structural helices implied have also been directly imaged using electron ptychography. Importantly, as lithium niobate is a uniaxial ferroelectric, the torsional strain in these structural helices necessarily also causes dipolar helices to form, inferred through consideration of pertinent piezoelectric tensors and flexoelectric coefficients. Helices are topologically distinct from the more commonly reported vortices and, importantly, they are chiral. Helical (and hence chiral) character was confirmed by observing that DPC images were identical before and after the sample was inverted. Chirality was also established through second harmonic optical circularly-polarised dichroism measurements, in which unusually large interfacial signals were seen. It must be stressed that the arrays of helices observed are distinct from moir\'e patterns; they facilitate lattice rotation combining plastic and elastic deformation and are not simply a superposition of lattices, twisted with respect to one another. Thus, intimately bonded twisted oxide interfaces will have distinctly different characteristics from those of twisted stacks of two-dimensional van der Waals materials, opening up a new and distinct kind of twistronics.</p></description>

In particular, Kramers-Weyl fermions, spin-split Fermi surfaces probed through quantum oscillations and quantum geometric nonlinear Hall and intrinsic spin Hall responses have garnered significant attention. Despite progress in understanding these phenomena individually, their coexistence with topological surface states, Fermi arcs and chirality dependent quantum geometric transport remains scarce, as pronounced responses involve suitable symmetries, SOC and Fermi surface geometry. Here, we explore this synergy in experimentally synthesized WAl$_2$, considering both structural enantiomers using first-principles calculations and symmetry analysis. We observed twelve Kramers-Weyl (KW) crossings with quantized chiral charges $|C|=1$ and $|C|=3$, accompanied by nontrivial surface states and Fermi arcs. The pronounced metallic character gives rise to six Fermi surface sheets exhibiting antisymmetric SOC, with distinct extremal orbits and candidate spin-split pairs resolved through calculated de Haas-van Alphen (dHvA) quantum oscillations. The electronic structure also exhibits large intrinsic Berry curvature dipole (BCD) arising from the asymmetric distribution of Berry curvature, giving rise to a nonlinear Hall response. The opposite structural handedness of the two enantiomers reverses the chiralities and BCD, reversing the direction of Fermi arcs and nonlinear Hall current. BCD attains $|D_{zz}|\approx0.338$, yielding nonlinear Hall current densities $|j_x|\approx5.04\times10^{10}~\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$ and $|j_y|\approx2.52\times10^{10}~\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. We observe enhanced SHC associated with triply charged KW point at $\Gamma$, suggesting role of higher Chern number in the SHC.</p></description>

      <title>[8] Sliding-ferroelectric control of dipolar and quadrupolar excitons in R-stacked WSe2</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26158</link>
      <description><p><b>Last authors:</b> Oleg V. Yazyev, Andras Kis</p><p><b>Authors:</b> Asmund Ottesen, Shun Feng, Edoardo Lopriore, et al.</p><p><span style='display:inline-block;padding:4px 9px;border-radius:999px;background:#fee2e2;color:#991b1b;font-weight:700;'>Score 8/10</span> <b>B_IMPORTANT_CONDMAT</b></p><p><b>Why:</b> Experimental study on exciton control and transport in few-layer 2D heterostructures.</p><p><b>Tags:</b> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#2Dmaterials</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#heterostructure</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#excitons</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#ferroelectricity</span> <span style='display:inline-block;margin:2px 4px 2px 0;padding:2px 6px;border-radius:999px;background:#eef2ff;color:#3730a3;font-size:12px;'>#opticalspectroscopy</span></p><p><img src='https://arxiv.org/static/browse/0.3.4/images/arxiv-logo-fb.png' style='max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:10px;' /></p><hr/><p><b>Abstract:</b> A fundamental property of interlayer excitons is their dipolar character, enabling electrical tunability, enhanced exciton-exciton interactions and extended lifetime. It is important for studying collective phenomena and realizing novel optoelectronic devices. However, in homo- or heterostructures based on two-dimensional semiconductors, the magnitude and orientation of the dipole moment are commonly locked due to spatially confined charges and nature of the band transition. Here, we use gate-dependent photoluminescence of few-layer R-WSe2 to harness sliding ferroelectricity for controlling the exciton dipole configuration of emerging layer-hybridised excitons. The sliding-ferroelectric control enables a pronounced on/off switching of the diffusive transport of hybrid dipolar excitons, while further facilitating gradual and abrupt dipole reconfigurations with emerging quadrupolar excitons. Our optical probe reveals intermediate states of vertically aligned interfacial polarisation with magnitudes that confirm cumulative polarisation in multilayers. Overall, our work presents sliding ferroelectricity as a powerful tool to tune interlayer coupling and layer hybridisation. These results represent a step toward ferroelectric-controlled exciton interconnects and novel multi-bit optical memories.</p></description>
